title: Data sources for browser statistics practice
text:
The browser statistics activities use a synthetic practice record, an observational record of secondary-school students, an invented feedback-by-practice quiz record, a published reading instruction record, and archived numerical scores used in an invented factorial teaching setting. Each supports a different kind of comparison. This note explains what the records contain, where they come from, and how they may be reused.
Use this list to find the data for your chapter; the sections below give downloads, column explanations, source context, and reuse terms.
Use short, meaningful names in your code. Keep starting data in d0 and a working copy in dat when changing rows. Report calculated statistical results to four decimal places, keeping full precision for calculations. Input precision or software rounding may slightly change the last digits.
Four CSV files are available below. Each uses a comma as the delimiter and has variable names in its first row. The reading instruction data are obtained directly from the carData R package; no extract of that dataset accompanies this note. The reading instruction and review-timing records remain available for reference consumers and the shared workspace; the Chapter 4 page uses the feedback and practice scores instead.

title: Data sources for browser statistics practice
text:
Synthetic Special Practice record
Download the Special Practice data (CSV)
This QMSBR record contains 120 fictional participants: 60 assigned to Special Practice and 60 to Usual Practice. The imagined study compares two practice formats with four sessions and equal total study time. A common assessment, scored from 0 to 40 points, takes place two weeks later. These are constructed teaching records, not observations from an actual experiment.







Field
Meaning and coding




id
Artificial row identifier, C3-001 through C3-120; it has no personal meaning.


group
Special Practice or Usual Practice, with 60 records in each condition.


score
Integer score on the common delayed assessment, in points on a 0–40 scale.



The concise headers id, group, and score replace the earlier student_id, assigned_condition, and delayed_score headers. The records and their order are unchanged.
All 120 records are retained, and the three fields contain no missing values. The comparison direction is Special Practice minus Usual Practice. The assignment and follow-up details belong to the invented study description; the values alone do not establish a research design.
The supplied rows define a fixed teaching record. Calculate software results from those rows and retain their full precision during analysis. Use these records for CSV tasks and the inputs supplied in each core exercise for its calculations.
Reuse. QMSBR dedicates this synthetic CSV to the public domain under CC0 1.0 Universal. The dedication applies to the CSV. Retain its description as synthetic when presenting or adapting it.

title: Data sources for browser statistics practice
text:
UCI Student Performance extract
Download the UCI groups data (CSV)
This extract retains all 395 records from the mathematics file in Paulo Cortez’s Student Performance dataset. The source records concern students in two Portuguese secondary schools. Higher-education intention was observed, not assigned. One row represents one recorded student.
Source and attribution. Cortez, P. (2008). Student Performance [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5TG7T. The UCI dataset page provides the source files and variable documentation.
QMSBR prepared this three-column extract through a curated copy of the mathematics data. All rows remain in their source order. The adaptations are the addition of an artificial identifier, selection and renaming of fields, and derivation of pass status from the recorded final grade.







Field
Source, meaning, and transformation




id
Artificial identifier U001 through U395, added by QMSBR as student_id in the curated copy and renamed here. It is not an original participant identifier.


higher
Source field higher, retained as higher_education in the curated copy and renamed here. yes means the student reported an intention to pursue higher education; no means the student reported no such intention.


pass
Derived from source final grade G3, retained as pass in the curated copy and renamed here. Yes means a grade of at least 10 on the 0–20 scale; No means a grade below 10.



The three supplied fields have no missing values. There are 375 yes intention records and 20 no intention records. For a passing proportion within an intention group, use that group’s total as the denominator. The comparison direction is intention yes minus intention no, with the result interpreted as an observed association in this record.
Recorded zero grades. The source documentation marks the dataset as having no missing values, but the source mathematics file contains an unresolved pattern: 38 records have final grade zero and zero absences, and 25 of those also have a positive second-period grade. The documentation does not establish a common meaning for all these zeros. The primary comparison retains grades as recorded. Omitting the zero-grade records is a diagnostic check that changes the analysed set, rather than an established correction.
Grades and absences are absent from this three-column extract. It therefore cannot identify the zero-grade records or reproduce that diagnostic exclusion. Interpret any supplied diagnostic results alongside this limitation.
Reuse. The source and this extract are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. When redistributing or adapting the extract, credit Cortez and the UCI Machine Learning Repository, retain the source and licence links, and identify QMSBR’s adaptations and any further changes you make. The licence does not imply endorsement by the source creators.

title: Data sources for browser statistics practice
text:
Feedback and practice quiz scores
Download the feedback and practice data (CSV)
This QMSBR record contains 24 invented Grade 7 students, each measured once on a fractions quiz scored from 0 to 20. The imagined study crosses three feedback conditions with two practice schedules, giving six cells of four different students. The Chapter 4 page uses the 12 Massed-practice rows for its one-way example and all 24 rows for the full factorial model.







Field
Meaning and coding




student
Sequential identifier 1–24; it has no personal meaning.


feedback
Rereading, Answer feedback or Explanatory feedback, in that teaching order.


practice
Massed or Spaced, in that teaching order.


score
Integer quiz score in points on a 0–20 scale.



A CSV stores these labels as plain text, so R orders them alphabetically unless the script declares the order. Every analysis sets levels = c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback") and levels = c("Massed", "Spaced") with factor() before fitting a model.
The 24 scores are fixed authored values, not a sample generated at render time, and the repeated residual pattern is deliberate so the arithmetic stays visible. They are teaching records: they do not validate a Normal model, equal variances, or any real effect of feedback or practice scheduling. There are no missing values and no student appears twice.
Maintained provenance. The canonical file, its complete score table and the full preparation record belong to the Chapter 4 technical document in the course materials, under its data section ch04-data-feedback-practice. This page redistributes only the identity and dictionary its readers need; the copy here is verified byte for byte against that canonical file.
Reuse. QMSBR dedicates this synthetic CSV to the public domain under CC0 1.0 Universal. Retain its description as invented teaching data when presenting or adapting it.

title: Data sources for browser statistics practice
text:
Reading instruction data from carData
This reference example uses Baumann from carData: Companion to Applied Regression Data Sets, by John Fox, Sanford Weisberg, and Brad Price. The package documentation for Baumann describes 66 records with a group field, two pretests, and three post-tests. It traces the teaching dataset to Moore and McCabe’s Introduction to the Practice of Statistics (2nd ed., 1993, pp. 794–795).
Once carData is available in R or WebR, load the dataset explicitly and prepare a working copy with the activity’s group labels:
data("Baumann", package = "carData")
d0 <- Baumann
dat <- d0
dat$score <- dat$post.test.1
dat$group <- factor(
  dat$group,
  levels = c("Basal", "DRTA", "Strat"),
  labels = c("DRA", "DRTA", "Think-aloud")
)
This code keeps the package record in d0, copies it to dat, gives the selected outcome the short name score, and changes the working group labels. It retains all 66 observed records and their scores. The outcome used here is post.test.1, the selected error-detection score in points on a 0–16 scale. The original package object remains available as Baumann.

The study description and assignment counts come from Baumann, Seifert-Kessell, and Jones (1992), Effect of Think-Aloud Instruction on Elementary Students’ Comprehension Monitoring Abilities, particularly the Method section on printed page 147. The study assigned 68 fourth-grade children in one rural Midwestern school. One child in each innovative condition had an unavailable outcome because of illness or transfer. The package therefore contains 66 observed outcomes, with 22 per group; it provides no scores for the two unavailable outcomes.
The reference example selects one outcome and uses an unadjusted one-way model with a common within-group variance. The source study used several outcomes and pretest-adjusted analyses. Its integrated success criterion is invented for an imagined future replication: both DRA-referenced contrasts must have lower endpoints above zero in a two-sided 95% Bonferroni family. Applying that criterion to these historical records is a post hoc teaching analysis. It is not a prespecified decision attributed to the original investigators. Linking complete-outcome calculations to effects for all assigned children also requires a justification for the unavailable outcomes; a completion check alone does not establish that link.
Source and reuse. The browser obtains carData from the WebR package repository at run time. This note distributes no Baumann CSV or package copy. The package retains its upstream GPL version 2 or later terms, as stated on its CRAN page. Anyone redistributing the package or a derived extract should retain the applicable upstream terms and notices. The research article is cited, not redistributed, and its publication terms are separate from the package’s terms.

title: Data sources for browser statistics practice
text:
Review-timing data
Download the review-timing data (CSV) · Full codebook
This 36-case file preserves every score, factor code and case order from the generic SPSS_2way.sav in the 6020-25F26S teaching archive. The donor columns were Score, A and B. QMSBR added a sequential identifier and gave the factors the labels below. The Grade 7 fractions lesson, resource descriptions, review times, quiz interpretation and random assignment are invented for Chapter 4. The archived scores themselves were not newly simulated, and the source file does not document a real educational study or establish randomization.







Field
Meaning and coding




student
Added sequential case identifier, 1–36.


resource
Original A: 1 = Textbook, 2 = Tutorial, 3 = Video.


timing
Original B: 1 = Same day, 2 = Two days, 3 = One week.


score
Original Score, unchanged. Values range from 7 to 20; the invented setting interprets them as numbers correct on a 20-item retention quiz.



There are four complete cases in each of the nine cells and no missing values. Scores sum to 407. In resource order Textbook, Tutorial, Video and timing order Same day, Two days, One week, cell means are (8.5000, 9.0000, 8.2500), (15.7500, 14.2500, 18.2500) and (9.7500, 9.7500, 8.2500). A full resource-by-timing model fits these records under independent-student, common-variance working assumptions. Normal errors give the exact classical F and t references. These archived scores are kept for reference consumers and the shared workspace; the Chapter 4 page does not use them.
Source and reuse. Retain the archived-file attribution and identify the educational setting as invented when adapting this example. The CC0 dedication for the separate Special Practice CSV does not apply to these archived scores. This note assigns no new licence to the donor file; QMSBR’s original descriptions and code retain the terms in LICENSE.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Use these short examples beside Chapter 3 and its lecture, or adapt them while working on an exercise, Computer Lab or homework. Computer Lab 3 uses one Special Practice comparison and a change from 95% to 90% confidence in the final classroom activity round. This page is a selectable reference menu, not a checklist: choose the example the assigned work needs. Choose one software route: R here, desktop R, or the lab’s SPSS instructions. The lab contains the activity and its worked answers; this page supplies reusable method support.
Everything here uses base R with the standard stats and graphics commands. No package is loaded or installed. Choose Run All to run a complete example. Start Over restores that cell’s starting code. Calculate at full precision and report statistical results to four decimal places. Rounded inputs or different software rounding choices can produce small differences in the last digits. For keyboard shortcuts and individual commands, see how to run code.
Use the assigned task’s own data and settings. Each example includes its own setup and can start on its own; the cells and the workspace have separate R objects, so copy the whole cell when you move code. Fixed code and output remain readable if the browser R runtime cannot start.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Before you start
A command is one instruction for R, such as mean(score). An object is a named value R keeps for later, such as score. The assignment arrow <- creates one: score <- 60 stores 60 under the name score, and typing score on its own line prints it. c() combines several values into one vector, so c(50, 54, 48) holds three scores. $ takes one named column out of a table: dat$score is the score column of dat. A function is a command that does a job, written with its arguments inside the brackets. In t.test(special, usual, var.equal = FALSE) the first two arguments supply the data and var.equal = FALSE is a named setting; commas separate them, and text in quotes is a label rather than an object. Names must match exactly, so Mean is not mean. See how to run code for the buttons and keyboard shortcuts, and for what to do when R reports an error.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Normal areas and z scores
A z score reports how many SDs a value lies from its mean: z <- (score - mu) / sigma. pnorm(z) returns the lower-tail area below z under the standard Normal curve, and pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE) returns the area above it. qnorm(p) reverses the question: it returns the cutoff whose lower-tail area is p. An area between two bounds is the difference of their cumulative probabilities, so pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1) gives the central area within one SD.








The z score is 2.0000, with lower area .9772 and upper area .0228. The central areas are .6827, .9545 and .9973, and the central-95% bounds are -1.9600 and 1.9600. Changing score moves one value’s position; changing a confidence level changes a reference cutoff. Neither turns an individual SD into the SE of a mean.

title: Chapter 3 R support
section: Build an interval from supplied values
text:
Build an interval from supplied values
Core Exercise 4 supplies the estimate, SE and critical value below. Use them to calculate its 95% interval. The book explains the approximate Welch procedure and how to interpret the interval.
<- stores a value under a name. c() joins values. Arithmetic works element by element, so c(-1, 1) subtracts and adds the margin to make the two endpoints. sprintf("%.4f", interval) displays four decimal places, including trailing zeros. It returns text for reporting; the numeric object interval keeps its full precision for later calculations.








The interval is [0.8571, 5.3429] points. For a small programming experiment, change only estimate to 2.1 and rerun. Both endpoints move down by one point while the width stays the same. Restore estimate <- 3.1 before answering the exercise.

title: Chapter 3 R support
section: One mean: known SD or estimated SD
text:
One mean: known SD or estimated SD
These are two different assumptions about the SD, shown with the same numerical spread. A stipulated population SD of 5 gives a z calculation; a sample SD of 5 from 25 observations gives a t calculation with n - 1 degrees of freedom. pt() returns a t-distribution probability, so 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), n - 1) is a two-sided p-value. Choose the procedure from what is actually known about the SD. Do not switch to the other one because it crosses a significance threshold.








Both statistics are 2.0000; the z p-value is .0455 and the t(24) p-value is .0569. These summaries do not reconstruct 25 unobserved raw scores. With an actual vector of scores, t.test(x, mu = 50) performs the same one-sample t test from the data themselves.

Numbers and a known SD
For a supplied vector of scores, length(), mean() and sd() return the count, average and sample SD. sqrt() takes a square root. Copy these commands into your workspace to try them:
scores <- c(12, 15, 17, 18, 20)
length(scores)
mean(scores)
sd(scores)
sigma <- 4
se <- sigma / sqrt(length(scores))
se
Here sigma is a separately stipulated population SD, while sd(scores) describes the entered sample. Homework 9 supplies its own complete code, scores, known SD and critical value. Use those inputs for its interval. Native R output can show a different number of digits; use four decimals when recording calculated results.


Sample size and the t reference
Hold the mean difference and the SD fixed and change only the sample size, so the SE and the degrees of freedom are the only moving parts. data.frame() places the results side by side in one small table. These are two stipulated summaries for two hypothetical samples; a larger real dataset would not keep exactly the same mean and SD, and a large sample must never be created by duplicating the same observations.








The SE falls from 1.5811 to 0.5000, the statistic rises from 1.2649 to 4.0000, and the reference distribution changes from t(9) to t(99). This comparison is about precision and the reference tail; it is not a rule for choosing a test at some fixed sample size.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Compare two groups
The Special Practice CSV has 120 fictional participants, 60 per assigned condition, with complete delayed assessment scores on a 0-40 scale. The data note gives the invented design and explains the CSV’s relationship to the book.
read.csv() reads the named file into a table. $ chooses a column; == matches a label, and [] selects the scores with that label. table() counts the groups and head(dat) shows the first six rows. Keep the original data in d0 and use dat as the working copy for every later calculation.
t.test(special, usual) compares the first mean minus the second. var.equal = FALSE requests Welch’s unequal-variances procedure and var.equal = TRUE pools the two variances; conf.level sets the confidence level. The returned object contains the test and interval; $stderr selects its estimated SE and $conf.int its endpoints.








The difference is 3.1000 points, the Welch SE about 1.1324 and the Welch 95% interval about [0.8575, 5.3425]. With this balanced CSV the two SEs coincide, while the degrees of freedom (about 117.51 against 118) and the critical values differ slightly. That arithmetic coincidence does not establish equal population variances. Compare the method labels, df and conditions rather than only which p-value is smaller. The Computer Lab uses the Welch procedure and its confidence change below.

Read the printout line by line
Every t.test() result prints in the same fixed layout, so reading this one carefully makes the others familiar. This is the welch output from the cell above, unchanged.
    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  special and usual
t = 2.7376, df = 117.51, p-value = 0.007152
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.8574549 5.3425451
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y
     27.1      24.0

The first line names the procedure: Welch’s two-sample t test, the unequal-variances one. Running the pooled call prints Two Sample t-test instead.
data: names the two vectors in the order you gave them, so the comparison is Special minus Usual.
On the fourth line, t = 2.7376 is the test statistic, df = 117.51 its degrees of freedom and p-value = 0.007152 the two-sided p-value, which is .0072 to four decimals. The df are fractional because Welch approximates them from the two sample variances; the pooled call reports 118.
The alternative hypothesis: line states what that p-value is calculated against: a true difference of zero, with both tails counted.
The two numbers under 95 percent confidence interval: are the interval endpoints, [0.8575, 5.3425] points. welch$conf.int returns the same pair, and conf.level changes them.
Under sample estimates:, mean of x 27.1000 and mean of y 24.0000 are the two group means. Their difference, 3.1000 points, is the estimate the interval is built around.

The printout does not show the SE. welch$stderr returns it: 1.1324 points. The interval is the estimate plus and minus the critical value for those df times that SE, which is how the interval and the test use the same quantities.


One confidence change
In the two-group example, level <- 0.95 sets the confidence level. Change only that line to level <- 0.90 and choose Run All. Read the new interval in welch$conf.int; diff(welch$conf.int) gives its width. Compare it with the original interval, then restore level <- 0.95. The same participants and scores supply the estimate, SE and two-sided p-value. A narrower interval at a lower confidence level reflects a different coverage requirement; it adds no observations or information.
The row and display changes below are reference examples. Use the change specified in your task rather than completing every variation.


Use supplied summary values
For core Exercise 2, enter its group counts and sample SDs directly. ^2 squares each SD; division by its group count gives that group’s contribution to the working variance. Add them before taking the square root. Copy this short calculation into your workspace.
n1 <- 60
n0 <- 60
s1 <- 6.0
s0 <- 6.4
sqrt(s1^2 / n1 + s0^2 / n0)
The same formula covers an unbalanced reference case: change only one declared group count, such as n0 <- 40, and read the larger SE. That is a reference step with stipulated summaries, not a new dataset.


Change the data and rerun
Replace only dat <- d0 in the two-group cell with the following line, then choose Run All to rerun the complete calculation:
dat <- d0[-(1:3), ]
1:3 means rows 1 through 3. A negative row index removes those rows; the empty place after the comma keeps all columns. Alternatively, use:
dat <- head(d0, -3)
head() with a negative count keeps all except the last three rows. The file begins with Special Practice and ends with Usual Practice, so the alternatives affect different groups. Keep both groups populated. Rerun the whole cell and compare group counts, means, the difference, SE and interval. Restore dat <- d0 and rerun to recover the starting result. These file-order exclusions change the analysed records; they are programming experiments, not random sampling or a remedy for missingness.
For a task that reverses the comparison, reverse both the t.test() inputs and the explicit subtraction in the line that prints difference. Multiplying both score vectors by the same positive number changes the measurement units. Use the complete script and settings supplied with that task.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Paired scores
These eight invented students were measured before and after one short practice session, on the same score scale at both times. They are not Special Practice records. Define the difference difference <- after - before before calculating anything, so the direction is after minus before.
paired = TRUE tells t.test() to analyse the within-student differences. The second call performs the same one-sample test on the differences themselves, and returns the same statistic, df, p-value and interval.








The mean difference is 2.0000 with SD 2.0000 and SE 0.7071, giving t(7) = 2.8284, p = .0255 and the 95% interval [0.3280, 3.6720]. The paired SE uses the variance of the differences, which subtracts twice the covariance between the two measurements; the independent-samples formula omits that covariance because it describes a different design. A before-and-after difference alone cannot separate the session from time trends, repeated testing or other concurrent changes.

A connected paired-score plot
cbind() places the two measurement columns side by side and t() transposes them, so each student becomes one column with two rows. matplot() then draws one line per student across the two measurement positions. type = "b" draws both points and lines, xaxt = "n" suppresses the default numeric axis, and axis() labels positions 1 and 2.








Each line joins the same student across measurements. Most lines rise, one is flat and one falls; the paired test summarizes those eight within-student changes rather than two separate group averages.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Covariance and correlation
cov(x, y) reports how two measurements vary together in their original product units, so its size depends on the measurement scale. cor(x, y) divides by both SDs and is unit free, between -1 and 1. Multiplying x by 10 is a positive unit change: the covariance is multiplied by 10 while the Pearson correlation is unchanged. method = "spearman" correlates the ranks instead of the values and describes monotonic association, as introduced in Chapter 2.








The covariance 28.1429 becomes 281.4286 while Pearson’s r stays .9599; the Spearman rank correlation is .9222. These are the same eight paired scores used above. A correlation describes association in these records; it establishes no causal direction and is not a regression coefficient.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Base R graphs
 Each graph below runs in its own cell with its own data-loading line, so you can run any one of them on its own. All of them use base graphics; no plotting package is needed. Read the axis labels and the statistic being displayed before interpreting a picture.

A histogram of all scores
hist() counts observations within score intervals. breaks = 10 is a suggestion for the number of intervals, main titles the plot and xlab names the horizontal axis. The bar heights are counts, not probabilities.








This histogram pools both practice groups, so a difference between them is not visible here.


A smoothed density curve
density() smooths the same scores into a continuous curve, and plot() draws it. The curve’s shape depends on the smoothing bandwidth reported in its output; it is an estimate, not the recorded data.










Boxplots by group
In score ~ group, ~ reads as “by”: one box per group label. A box shows the median and quartiles, the whiskers reach most of the remaining values, and separate points mark values far from the box.








The grouped boxplot makes the group structure visible that the pooled histogram hides. Its line is the median, not the mean estimated by the t comparison above.


A bar chart of two categories
These counts are one 50-person row of the count table below: the online participants who completed and who did not. barplot() draws one bar per named count, and ylab names the axis.










The same two categories as a pie
pie() shows the same two counts as shares of the 50 online participants. Bar lengths support more accurate comparison than pie angles, so prefer the bar chart when the exact sizes matter.








The denominator is the 50 online participants only. Do not draw the four cells of the two-by-two table as though they were four independent participation categories.


A scatterplot of two measurements
plot(x, y) draws one point per pair. abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2) adds a dashed line with intercept 0 and slope 1, marking equal scores: points above it improved and points below it declined.








The points rise together, which is the association summarized by covariance and correlation; their distance from the dashed line is the within-student change tested in the paired example.

title: Chapter 3 R support
text:
Run a supplied exercise script
The Computer Lab supplies the complete Special Practice script. Other exercises or their reference material supply any UCI or private HSB setup they use. If a script uses a bare CSV filename, open that CSV in the workspace first, or change its first file path to the public data/... path shown with the example. Paste all the setup and analysis into the workspace and run it together. Public CSVs listed on this page are already available there as data/...; on desktop R, keep that subfolder or change the path to your downloaded file. The supplied homework 9 code needs no CSV.
For variations in a supplied script, t.test(x, mu = ...) compares one mean with a stated value; paired = TRUE uses matched differences, var.equal = TRUE pools the variances and alternative states the test’s direction. Choose those settings from the study and the assigned question. pnorm() returns a Normal probability; qt() returns a t critical value. The chapter and task specify the model and any supplied critical value.

The worked count table
matrix(..., nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE) fills two rows in order, and dimnames names the rows and columns. Here the rows are the two participation formats and the columns are completion and its absence. prop.table(counts, 1) divides by each row’s total, so the two row proportions use the 50-person denominators. chisq.test(..., correct = FALSE) requests the ordinary Pearson calculation; the default two-by-two continuity correction answers a related but different question. $expected shows the counts predicted when format and completion are independent.








The completion proportions are .6400 and .3600, a difference of .2800 in the Online-minus-In-person order. All four expected counts are 25, giving X-squared 7.8400 with 1 df and p = .0051. These are invented records for an association question: participation format was not assigned, so the result supports no causal claim. Exercise 7 has its own table and counts; use its numbers, not these.
For a task using UCI data, run its complete CSV setup and coding. Its three-field extract contains no raw grades or absences, so the zero-grade omission finding remains supplied output; this extract cannot reproduce that exclusion.


Open a private course CSV
In the workspace, choose Open a CSV and select the course-supplied hsb.csv. The file stays in the browser session. Opening it makes the file available; the first line of the supplied script then reads it:
hsb <- read.csv("hsb.csv")
names(hsb)
names() lists the columns. Keep the course’s numeric codes and run the task’s group/coding setup before the analysis. If the file has a different name, use that exact name in read.csv(). A saved R script does not contain the CSV records: reopen both files after reloading the page.


Function and software references
The R manuals give argument details for formatting results, t tests, CSV import, Normal probabilities, t critical values, covariance and correlation, table proportions and Pearson tests. For the graphs, see histograms, density estimates, boxplots, bar charts, pie charts, scatterplots and matrix plots. Every command on this page belongs to base R, stats or graphics, so desktop R needs no installation step for them.
For the Computer Lab’s SPSS route: recoding, Crosstabs cells and independent-samples t tests. Use the task’s settings with either software route. Data sources and reuse cover all public records and their limitations.

title: Chapter 4 R support
text:
Before you start
A command is one instruction for R, such as mean(feedback_data$score). An object is a named value R keeps for later, such as n. The assignment arrow <- creates one: n <- 24 stores 24 under the name n, and typing n on its own line prints it. c() combines several values into one vector, so c("Massed", "Spaced") holds two labels. A table of records is an object too: feedback_data <- read.csv("data/feedback_practice.csv") reads the 24 records into a table called feedback_data, and factor() with levels = then fixes the order the conditions are listed in. $ takes one named column out of a table: feedback_data$score is the score column. A function is a command that does a job, written with its arguments inside the brackets. In aov(score ~ feedback, data = massed) the formula is the first argument and data = massed is a named one; commas separate them, and text in quotes is a label rather than an object. Names must match exactly, so Score is not score. See how to run code for the buttons and keyboard shortcuts, and for what to do when R reports an error.

title: Chapter 4 R support
section: The data and a first plot
text:
The data and a first plot
The invented study gives 24 different Grade 7 students a fractions quiz scored from 0 to 20. Each student appears once, in one of six cells formed by three feedback conditions and two practice schedules, with four students per cell. The data note records the identity of the file and its invented setting.
The 24 records are stored in a CSV file with the columns student, feedback, practice and score. read.csv() reads that file into a data frame. A CSV holds plain text with no order of its own, so the two factor() lines set each factor’s display and model order explicitly; without them R would sort alphabetically and put “Answer feedback” first. head() shows the first six rows, str() reports each column’s type and a factor’s level order, and table() with two factors counts the six cells.








The table has 24 rows and four columns. str() confirms that feedback is a factor with three levels in the declared order and practice a factor with two, and the counted table shows six cells of four students. Every cell on this page repeats these same three setup lines. On desktop R, use read.csv("feedback_practice.csv") with the file beside your script.

The same 24 scores typed in
You do not need the file. Typing the scores keeps the whole record visible, which helps when you want to see exactly what is being analysed, or to change one score and rerun. data.frame() builds the table; rep(..., each = 8) repeats each feedback label eight times and the nested rep() alternates the two schedules in blocks of four. The same two factor() calls fix the level order, written here inside data.frame().








This produces the same 24 records, in the same order, as the CSV, so either starting point can feed the analyses below. The cells that follow all start from the CSV, because that is the shorter setup to repeat.


The Massed subset and every observation
The first comparison uses only the 12 Massed-practice students, so the three feedback conditions are compared under one schedule. subset() keeps the rows matching a condition. table() counts the three groups, and aggregate(score ~ feedback, ...) applies mean within each one; tapply() returns the same three means as a named vector.








There are 12 Massed students, four per group, with means 6.0000, 8.0000 and 10.0000 and the same SD 1.8257 in each group. The means differ by two points per step while the groups overlap.


A dotplot of the 12 scores
stripchart() draws every observation. method = "stack" stacks equal scores so none is hidden, pch chooses the point symbol, las = 1 keeps the group labels horizontal and par(mar = ...) widens the left margin for them. points() then adds the three group means as crosses.








With four scores per group the dots show the data more directly than a summary would. A chart of the three means alone would hide the overlap.


The same subset as boxplots
boxplot(score ~ feedback, ...) draws one box per group. With only four observations per group the box is a coarse summary, so read it beside the dotplot rather than instead of it.

title: Chapter 4 R support
text:
One-way ANOVA
aov() fits the model. In score ~ feedback, ~ separates the outcome from its grouping factor. summary() prints the ANOVA table: a row for the factor and a row for the within-group residuals.








The table gives F(2, 9) = 4.8000 with p = .0381. The null is that the three Massed group means are equal; the alternative is that at least two differ. Under independent observations, equal group error variances and Normal errors, the null ratio has an F(2, 9) reference. This result concerns the 12 invented Massed scores only.

Where the df and mean squares come from
deviance() returns the residual sum of squares and df.residual() the residual degrees of freedom, so their ratio is the within-group mean square MS_W. The between-group sum of squares 32 divided by its 2 df gives MS_B; the F statistic is the ratio of the two mean squares, and pf(..., lower.tail = FALSE) gives its right-tail probability.








SS_W is 30.0000 with 9 df, so MS_W is 3.3333. The three group means carry 2 df because the third is fixed once the grand mean and the other two are known, and each group of four residuals sums to zero, leaving 12 - 3 = 9. Both mean squares estimate the same error variance under the null; their ratio is not expected to be exactly 1 in an observed sample.

title: Chapter 4 R support
text:
Contrasts and multiple comparisons
A contrast gives each group mean a weight, with the weights summing to zero. Here c(-1, 1, 0) is Answer feedback minus Rereading and c(-1, 0, 1) is Explanatory feedback minus Rereading, in the declared feedback order. rbind() stacks the two weight rows; weights %*% group_means multiplies them out and drop() returns a plain named vector.
The SE of a contrast is sqrt(MS_W * sum(c^2 / n)): the weights are squared because variances of independent means add. sweep(weights^2, 2, group_n, "/") divides each squared weight by its own group count and rowSums() adds them. qt(1 - .05 / (2 * 2), df) is the Bonferroni critical value: the first 2 allows two tails and the second allows the two declared comparisons, giving at least 95% joint coverage under the model. State the family before choosing the multiplier.








Both comparisons have SE 1.2910 with 9 error df, and the Bonferroni critical value is 2.6850. The intervals are [-1.4663, 5.4663] for Answer minus Rereading and [0.5337, 7.4663] for Explanatory minus Rereading. Under the stated conditions the second excludes zero and the first does not; an interval containing zero does not establish equal means. The two intervals share the Rereading mean, so they are positively related.

All three pairs with Tukey
TukeyHSD() answers a different question: all three pairwise differences at once. Its family is larger than the two declared comparisons, so its multiplier and intervals differ. Run it in its own cell so the two families stay visibly separate.








The three differences are 2.0000, 4.0000 and 2.0000, with intervals [-1.6045, 5.6045], [0.3955, 7.6045] and [-1.6045, 5.6045] and adjusted p-values .3150, .0310 and .3150. Choose a family because it matches the question you asked, never because its intervals exclude zero.

title: Chapter 4 R support
text:
The full factorial model
Now use all 24 students. No one supplies an observation in both schedules, so these are six separate groups of four different students. In the model formula, feedback * practice includes both main effects and their interaction. tapply() with list() of the two factors returns the table of six cell means; rowMeans() and colMeans() give the equally weighted marginal means.








Six cells of four students leave 24 - 6 = 18 error df. Feedback gives F(2, 18) = 38.4000, practice gives F(1, 18) = 28.8000, and the interaction gives F(2, 18) = 9.6000 with p = .0015. The feedback marginal means are 6.0000, 10.0000 and 14.0000 and the practice marginal means are 8.0000 and 12.0000; these averages use equal weights across the other factor’s levels. With an interaction present, the cell means are needed to see the pattern that those averages summarize. The 12-record Massed analysis above used a slice of these data and had 9 error df, not 18.

Residuals from the factorial fit
A residual is one student’s score minus the fitted value for that student’s cell, so the residuals are what the six cell means leave unexplained. fitted() returns the fitted cell mean for each of the 24 students and resid() the matching residual. Plotting one against the other puts the cells side by side: plot() draws the points, abline(h = 0, lty = 2) adds a dashed horizontal line at zero, and table(round(resid(full_fit), 4)) counts how often each residual value occurs.








The points fall in five vertical columns, at fitted values 6, 8, 10, 12 and 18. Two cells share the fitted mean 6, so that column holds eight students; their residuals coincide exactly, so only four dots are visible there. Every cell contributes the residuals -2, -1, 1 and 2, which is why the counted table shows each of those four values six times while the plot shows twenty dots.
Look for three things. First, the points in each column should be centred on the dashed line; they are, because fitting cell means forces the residuals within a cell to sum to zero. Second, the vertical spread should be about the same at every fitted value: a fan that widens as the fitted mean grows would question the equal error variance the F tests assume. Third, a point far from all the others would mark an unusual observation worth checking in the data. With four scores per cell this display can show only a coarse pattern, and these invented scores are unusually regular; it supports the conditions rather than proving them.

title: Chapter 4 R support
text:
Eta squared for each source
Eta squared is a descriptive summary of magnitude: one source’s sum of squares divided by the total sum of squares. It reports the share of the observed squared variation that goes with that source in this sample. anova() on a fitted model returns the table whose "Sum Sq" column holds those sums, and rownames() supplies the source names, so full_SS / sum(full_SS) divides each one by the total.








In the 12-record Massed one-way fit, the between-group sum of squares is 32.0000 and the total is 62.0000, so eta squared is .5161. In the full factorial fit the sums of squares are 256.0000 for feedback, 96.0000 for practice, 64.0000 for the interaction and 60.0000 for the residuals, a total of 476.0000; the four shares are .5378, .2017, .1345 and .1261, and the exact shares add to one, although the four rounded values shown add to 1.0001 because each rounds up.
Read these as the fraction of variation among these observed scores, not as the fraction of learning caused by feedback. A value depends on the design and on which sources the model contains, so the one-way .5161 and the factorial .5378 are two different quantities rather than one quantity measured twice. If software reports partial eta squared instead, its denominator is that term’s own sum of squares plus the residual sum of squares, not the total; say which one you are reporting.

title: Chapter 4 R support
section: The interaction plot and one selected comparison
text:
The interaction plot and one selected comparison
interaction.plot(x.factor, trace.factor, response) calculates the cell means and joins them with one line per trace level. type = "b" draws points and lines, lty and col distinguish the three lines, trace.label names the legend and ylim fixes the score axis.








Each line joins means of different students; the lines are not repeated measurements. Nonparallel lines are descriptive evidence that the schedule comparison changes across feedback conditions. An inferential claim also needs uncertainty and a stated reference distribution.

Simple differences and a difference of differences
cell_means[, "Spaced"] - cell_means[, "Massed"] subtracts two columns of the cell-mean table, giving the schedule difference within each feedback condition. Subtracting two of those differences asks how the schedule comparison itself changes between two conditions. All four cell means come from different students, so under the full model their variances add and SE = sqrt(MS_E * (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4)).
Because this comparison is selected after looking at the plot, sqrt(2 * qf(.95, 2, error_df)) supplies a Scheffe multiplier covering every contrast in the two-degree-of-freedom interaction space. unname() drops an inherited label when printing; the value is unchanged.








The schedule differences are 0.0000, 4.0000 and 8.0000 points for Rereading, Answer feedback and Explanatory feedback. The selected difference of differences is 4.0000 with SE 1.8257, the Scheffe multiplier is 2.6663, and the simultaneous interval is [-0.8680, 8.8680]. It includes zero although the omnibus interaction p-value is .0015: the joint test addresses all interaction directions at once, while this interval covers every selected contrast in that space. The two procedures answer different questions with different calibrations, so neither one overrules the other. A simple effect within one condition also contains a practice main-effect component and lies outside this interaction-only family.

title: Chapter 4 R support
text:
Run a supplied script
Paste the whole script for an exercise, Computer Lab question or homework into your workspace, including its data-loading and factor() lines. The workspace has its own R session, so objects created in the cells above are not available there. The public CSV on this page is available in the workspace as data/feedback_practice.csv; on desktop R, keep that subfolder or change the path to your downloaded file. A script that types the 24 scores needs no file at all.
The complete starting script below runs in order in a fresh session and reproduces the page’s main factorial result, the cell means, the schedule differences and the selected simultaneous interval. Copy all of it, then change only what your own task requires.
feedback_data <- read.csv("data/feedback_practice.csv")
feedback_data$feedback <- factor(feedback_data$feedback,
  levels = c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback"))
feedback_data$practice <- factor(feedback_data$practice,
  levels = c("Massed", "Spaced"))
full_fit <- aov(score ~ feedback * practice, data = feedback_data)
summary(full_fit)
cell_means <- with(feedback_data,
                   tapply(score, list(feedback, practice), mean))
cell_means
schedule_difference <- cell_means[, "Spaced"] - cell_means[, "Massed"]
schedule_difference
selected <- schedule_difference["Answer feedback"] -
            schedule_difference["Rereading"]
error_df <- df.residual(full_fit)
MS_E <- deviance(full_fit) / error_df
selected_SE <- sqrt(MS_E * (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4))
scheffe <- sqrt(2 * qf(.95, 2, error_df))
c(estimate = unname(selected), SE = selected_SE, multiplier = scheffe)
sprintf("%.4f", unname(selected) + c(-1, 1) * scheffe * selected_SE)
Commands used in the supplied scripts include data.frame() and rep() for entering scores, subset() and droplevels() for a reduced set, aov() and summary() for a model, anova() for a fitted model’s table, deviance() and df.residual() for the error term, TukeyHSD() for all pairs, qt() and qf() for critical values, interaction.plot() and stripchart() for base graphs, and sprintf("%.4f", x) for reporting. sprintf() returns text; keep the numeric objects for further arithmetic. Use the family, weights and factor order declared by your task.

Open a private course CSV
Choose Open a CSV in the workspace and select the course-supplied hsb.csv. It remains in this browser session and is not uploaded. Read it with the first line of the task’s complete script:

names() shows the column names. Keep the course’s numeric codes and run the supplied group and coding setup, weights and model. Opening a file does not by itself create the R object. If you reload the page, reopen both the CSV and your saved script; saving a script does not save the CSV records.

Every command on this page belongs to base R, stats or graphics, so desktop R needs no installation step for them.

title: Your R workspace
text:
How to run code
Run a complete example. Click Run All to run the whole code block or workspace script, including its data-loading commands.
Try commands one by one. Click inside a code box and place the cursor on the first command. Press Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux or Command+Return on macOS, or click Run Code. This runs the current complete command and advances the cursor. Select several commands first to run just that selection. Enter/Return alone adds a new line.
Objects remain available for later commands in the same code box. An assignment such as dat <- d0 usually prints nothing; run head(dat) to inspect the result. A command spanning several lines, such as a model or plot call with several arguments, runs together. When selecting text, include the entire command; an incomplete selection produces an R error. After changing data, rerun every calculation that uses them. Start Over restores a chapter block’s original code and clears that block’s objects.
Use desktop RStudio. Put the complete code in an R script. With the cursor on a command, Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux or Command+Return on macOS runs the current line or selected code. Select the whole command when it spans several lines. The RStudio shortcut reference gives further details. In the R console, type a complete command and press Enter/Return. Run the data-loading commands before commands that use them.
If R shows an error. Read the last line of the message first: it usually names the problem, and nothing is damaged. Five common causes:

unexpected numeric constant or unexpected symbol: a missing comma between two values or arguments, such as c(50 54) instead of c(50, 54).
unexpected ‘)’: one closing bracket too many, such as c(50, 54)).
could not find function or a name R does not recognise: a misspelled name. R matches names exactly, so t.tset is not t.test and Mean is not mean.
A + prompt, or a result that never appears: an unmatched quote or bracket, so the command is still unfinished. Complete the quote or bracket, or press Esc to cancel, then run the command again.
object ‘dat’ not found: that object does not exist in this session, usually because its setup line has not been run. Rerun the cell’s setup lines, or choose Run All, before the command that uses the object.

Correct the line and run it again. If a code box has drifted too far from its starting code, Start Over restores it.

Saving and reopening work
Save your R script and results before leaving. The script includes unrun edits; the results file pairs the latest output with its code and the earlier executed commands. For a reproducible submission, keep all setup in the script, clear R objects, and use Run All before saving. Save plots separately. Submit through your course's usual system.
Reloading clears R objects and imported files. Reopen your CSV and saved script, then run it. On desktop R, use the folder containing your script and CSV as the working directory; built-in examples using data/... need that subfolder. For a stalled calculation, save your code and reload.
